about: Two courses fused, grouped by idea: Signals and systems 1 after Prechtl (2010), Vorlesungen über Signale und Systeme 1, TU Wien (continuous time), and Signals and systems 2 after Doblinger (2015), Zeitdiskrete Signale und Systeme, 3rd edition (discrete time). Each lab shows the continuous signal beside the discrete one where both exist. Laplace and z-transform, Bode diagrams, the state space and controllability are left to the Automation lab. Sections and page ranges are those of the two texts' tables of contents (read on 1 Nov 2026); equation numbers are not given yet, only sections. Practice answers are worked by hand, each naming its section; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

labs.title: Shifting and scaling time
labs.idea: Shift, reverse and scale the time axis: a signal only moves and stretches, a sequence scaled by M loses samples.
labs.law: y(t) = x(at − t0)    y[n] = x[Mn + n0]
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), section 1.2, pp. 5–12; Doblinger (2015), section 2.2, pp. 15–18

equations.note: scaled by a, shifted to start at t = t0/a
shift by a whole number of samples
keep every M-th sample (M a whole number)

practice.question: x[n] = 1 for n = 0 … 4 and 0 elsewhere. How many samples of y[n] = x[2n − 3] are not zero?
practice.solution: y[n] ≠ 0 where 0 ≤ 2n − 3 ≤ 4, so 1.5 ≤ n ≤ 3.5: n = 2 and n = 3. Two samples, x[1] and x[3]; x[0], x[2] and x[4] are lost.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 2.2

labs.title: Linearity and time invariance
labs.idea: Test a system: does the output of a sum equal the sum of the outputs, and does a delayed input give a delayed output?
labs.law: S{a x1 + b x2} = a S{x1} + b S{x2}    S{x(t − t0)} = y(t − t0)
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), section 1.4, pp. 18–23; Doblinger (2015), section 3.1, pp. 30–44

equations.eq: S{a x1 + b x2} = a S{x1} + b S{x2}

practice.question: An LTI system's step response is s(t) = (1 − e^(−t/τ)) V with τ = 1 s. The input is a pulse of height 1 from t = 0 to t = 1 s. What is the output at t = 2 s?
practice.solution: The pulse is a step minus a step delayed by 1 s. By linearity and time invariance y(t) = s(t) − s(t − 1 s), so y(2 s) = (1 − e^(−2)) − (1 − e^(−1)) = e^(−1) − e^(−2) = 0.2325 V.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 1.4

labs.title: Convolution
labs.idea: Flip the impulse response, slide it, multiply and add up: the output of any LTI system, integral or sum.
labs.law: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ    y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n − k]
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), section 1.5, pp. 24–28; Doblinger (2015), section 3.1, pp. 30–44

equations.eq: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ = (x ∗ h)(t)

practice.question: A pulse of height 1 and length 1 s enters a system with h(t) = e^(−t/τ) for t ≥ 0, τ = 0.5 s. What is y(t) at t = 1 s?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 1.5

labs.title: Random signals and correlation
labs.idea: White noise forgets at once; a low-pass gives it memory. Cross-correlation finds an echo buried in noise.
labs.law: r_xx[k] = E{x[n] x[n + k]}    σy² = σx² (1 − a)/(1 + a)
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), sections 1.3, 3.4 and 4.6, pp. 13–17, 80–83, 101–105; Doblinger (2015), section 3.1

equations.eq: σy² = σx² (1 − a)/(1 + a), r_yy[k]/r_yy[0] = a^|k|

practice.question: White noise of variance 1 passes through y[n] = 0.9 y[n − 1] + 0.1 x[n]. What is the output's variance?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 4.6

labs.title: Fourier series
labs.idea: A periodic signal is a sum of harmonics; at a jump, the partial sums always overshoot. A periodic sequence needs only N.
labs.law: x(t) = Σ c_k e^(j2πkt/T)    x[n] = (1/N) Σ X[k] e^(j2πkn/N)
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), chapter 5, pp. 108–121; Doblinger (2015), section 2.3, pp. 19–29

equations.eq: x(t) = Σₖ c_k e^(j2πkt/T),  c_k = (1/T) ∫_T x(t) e^(−j2πkt/T) dt
max of partial sum → 1 + 0.179 for a jump from −1 to 1

practice.question: A square wave jumps between −1 and +1. What is the amplitude of its third harmonic?
practice.solution: b_k = 4/(πk) for odd k, so b_3 = 4/(3π) = 0.424.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 5.1

labs.title: Fourier transform
labs.idea: Shorter in time is wider in frequency. A sequence has the same spectrum near zero, but repeated every sampling rate.
labs.law: X(f) = ∫ x(t) e^(−j2πft) dt    X(e^jΩ) = Σ x[n] e^(−jΩn)
labs.lecture: Prechtl (2010), sections 3.1–3.3, pp. 65–79; Doblinger (2015), section 4.1, pp. 67–73

practice.question: A pulse lasts 1 ms. At what frequency is its spectrum first zero?
practice.solution: X(f) = T sinc(fT) is zero where fT = 1, at f = 1/T = 1 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 3.1

labs.title: Harmonics and power
labs.idea: Harmonics in the current add RMS current and apparent power but no active power: they are distortion power.
labs.law: S² = P² + Q² + D²    THD = √(Σ_{k>1} I_k²) / I_1

equations.note: RMS of a current with harmonics

equations.eq: P = U I_1 cos φ_1,  Q = U I_1 sin φ_1
equations.note: with a sine voltage, only the fundamental carries P and Q

equations.eq: S = U I,  D = √(S² − P² − Q²)

practice.question: A 230 V sine voltage drives a current of 10 A (fundamental, in phase), 3 A at the third and 2 A at the fifth harmonic, all RMS. What is the RMS current?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 6.2

practice.question: For the same current, what is the distortion power D?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Prechtl (2010), section 6.3

labs.title: DFT, windows and the FFT
labs.idea: N samples give N lines that sample the spectrum; a sine between lines leaks, a window tames it, the FFT gets there fast.
labs.law: X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N)    Δf = fs/N

practice.question: A DFT of N = 1024 samples is taken at fs = 8 kHz. How far apart are its lines?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 7.1

labs.title: Sampling and aliasing
labs.idea: Sample fast enough and sincs rebuild the signal exactly; too slowly, and the samples fit a slower sine instead.
labs.law: x(t) = Σ x[n] sinc((t − nT)/T)    fs > 2 f_max

practice.question: A 7 kHz sine is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear?
practice.solution: 7 kHz is above fs/2 = 5 kHz; it folds to |7 − 10| kHz = 3 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 4.2

practice.question: Samples x[0] = 1 and all others 0 are rebuilt ideally. What is x(t) halfway between the first two samples?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 4.2

labs.title: Digital filters
labs.idea: An IIR filter from an analogue Butterworth by the bilinear transform, or an FIR filter from a windowed sinc.
labs.law: s = 2fs (z − 1)/(z + 1)    ωa = 2fs tan(π fc / fs)    h[n] = 2Fc sinc(2Fc (n − (N−1)/2)) w[n]

practice.question: A digital low-pass at fs = 8 kHz should cut off at 1 kHz by the bilinear transform. To what frequency is the analogue prototype pre-warped?
practice.solution: ωa = 2fs tan(π fc/fs) = 16000 tan(π/8) s⁻¹ = 6627 s⁻¹, so fa = ωa/2π = 1055 Hz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 6.3

practice.question: An ideal low-pass with normalised cut-off Fc = 0.125 has h[n] = 2Fc sinc(2Fc n). What is h[2]?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 6.2

labs.title: Changing the sampling rate
labs.idea: Keep every M-th sample and what lay above fs/(2M) folds into the band; filter first. Insert zeros, filter after.

equations.eq: y[n] = x[n/L] for n a multiple of L, else 0

practice.question: A 48 kHz signal is to be downsampled by M = 4. Up to what frequency may the anti-aliasing filter pass?
practice.solution: The new rate is 12 kHz, so the band must end at fs/(2M) = 6 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Doblinger (2015), section 8.2
